newsitem.title: DENMARK: Ruhrgas boss rejects gas regulator in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Ruhrgas boss rejects gas regulator in Germany.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, June 13, Reuter - Any attempt to force German gas companies to give up market share or to be supervised by a regulator as in Britain would lead to "a total regulatory mess," the head of Germany's largest gas company Ruhrgas AG said on Friday.
Burckhard Bergmann, vice chairman of Ruhrgas, was asked at a news conference if his company feared that under a regulator it could be forced to give up market share.
He replied that "a development like in the UK is impossible in Germany. You cannot force a private company to stay away from competition."
Bergmann pointed out that given there were 700 distribution companies in Germany "you would end up in Germany in a total regultory mess."
By contrast, when the UK gas market started to open up, former monopoly holder British Gas plc was forced to surrender market share and has since been closely supervised by regulator Ofgas.
Bergmann added that he believed German legislators took shared his view and were unlikely to impose such an obligation.
Market opening is a sensitive issue for Ruhrgas, which has a share of around 60 percent of Germany's 89 billion cubic metre (bcm) per year market.
The company is opposed to the European Union's proposed gas directive, which calls for the creation of a single demonopolised gas market.

Ruhrgas states in its annual report that "The draft directive provides among other things for gas companies to make their pipeline systems available to third parties, if necessary against their will. The gas industry rejects this...The Brussels draft creates more state regulation instead of more competition."
Ruhrgas bought around 55 bcm of gas in 1996, of which the largest share, 33 percent, came from Russia's Gazprom. But Bergmann appeared to rule out any possibility of entering the upstream in Russia.

"We have a long term relationship with Gazprom and are satisfied with it," he said. "Gazprom does the production and transport, and we do the marketing. We have no plans to go into the upstream, although if Gazprom asked us to we would consider it very carefully."

He later added that Gazprom was inviting foreign companies to participate in the upstream in frontier areas where their main contribution would be new technology, not an area in which Ruhrgas has great expertise. "Ruhrgas tries to behave so we do what we know," he said.
All gas Ruhrgas takes from Russia is delivered through Ukraine, and Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev said recently that the Ukrainian pipeline system needed rehabilitating.
Asked if Ruhrgas was keen to get involved in that programme, Bergmann said it was not really an issue for his company as Gazprom was responsible for transport as far as the German border.

But he did add that Ruhrgas has had initial discussions about possible involvement by western companies in rehabilitating the Ukrainian system with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
He denied reports in the Ukrainian press that Ruhrgas was definitely to participate in the privatisation of the Ukrainian network.

"We have not yet seen a concrete step from the Ukrainian government. If it came, we would consider it - I say that totally neutrally," he said. -- Sebastian Alison, Copenhagen Newsroom, +44 33 96 96 50
